questions.question: GHCi is given the expression "Hello World" directly (no putStrLn). Why does it echo back "Hello World" WITH the quotation marks, rather than printing the bare words?
options: GHCi always adds quotation marks around any output as decoration
GHCi is showing the Haskell-readable representation of the String value you entered, and that representation includes the quotes that mark it as a String
Because the string is exactly two words long
putStrLn was called implicitly and it always shows quotes
questions.explanation: Entering a bare expression at the GHCi prompt evaluates it and shows the result using its readable (Show) representation. For a String, the readable representation is the quoted form — the same text you would write in source code to produce that value.
optionFeedback: Quotation marks are not decoration added to everything — try `ghci> 42`, which prints as `42` with no quotes at all.
Length is irrelevant; a one-word or ten-word string is shown with quotes the same way.
putStrLn was not called here at all — GHCi's default echo-back behaviour is what adds the quotes, and putStrLn actually removes them, as later sections show.

questions.question: putStr "CSI" is run, immediately followed by putStr "243". What appears on the terminal?
options: CSI\n243\n (each on its own line)
CSI243 (both on the same line, since putStr never adds a newline)
A type error, because putStr can only be called once per program
243CSI, because the second call overwrites the first
questions.explanation: putStr writes exactly the characters it is given and adds no newline. Two putStr calls in sequence leave the cursor exactly where the first one finished, so the second call's characters continue directly on the same line.
optionFeedback: A newline only appears if something explicitly adds one, such as putStrLn — putStr never does.
putStr can be called as many times as you like within a do block; there is no such restriction.
Terminal output is not overwritten by later prints — each call appends its characters after whatever was already written.

questions.question: print "Hello World" and putStrLn "Hello World" both eventually reach the terminal. Why do they NOT display the same thing?
options: They actually do display exactly the same thing
print applies show first, and show's representation of a String includes its surrounding quotation marks, which putStrLn's direct String output never adds
print is slower, so extra characters appear from lag
putStrLn only works on String literals, while print works on the same value but converts it to a number first
questions.explanation: print n is equivalent to putStrLn (show n). show "Hello World" produces the String "\"Hello World\"" (quotes included, since that's the readable representation of a String), and putStrLn then displays those quote characters as part of the line. putStrLn "Hello World" skips show entirely and writes the characters as-is, with no added quotes.
optionFeedback: They differ specifically in the presence of quotation marks around the text — compare the exact output blocks shown above.
This is not a timing or performance effect; it is a difference in what text is actually produced.
putStrLn accepts any String value, not just literals, and print does not convert text to a number — it shows the value in its Haskell-readable form, which for a String includes quotes.

questions.question: Inside a real program's do block (not the GHCi prompt), the line `show 42` appears on its own, with its result unused. What happens?
options: 42 is printed to the terminal, just as it would be at the GHCi prompt
The String "42" is computed and then discarded; nothing is printed, because show performs no IO by itself and GHCi's auto-echo behaviour does not apply inside a compiled do block
It is a compile-time error, because show cannot appear inside a do block
It prints "42" including the quotation marks
questions.explanation: GHCi's habit of showing you the value of a typed expression is a feature of the interactive prompt, not a property of show itself. show is a pure function: it returns a String value. Inside an actual do block, an unused pure value is simply thrown away — nothing appears on the terminal unless an IO action like putStrLn actually uses it.
optionFeedback: That auto-display only happens at the interactive GHCi prompt; it is not something show does on its own inside a program.
show can appear inside a do block — the issue is not a parse or type error, it is that its result, a pure value, is simply unused and produces no visible effect.
Nothing is printed at all in this scenario, so no text — quoted or otherwise — appears.

questions.question: print :: Show a => a -> IO () is read as 'for a displayable type a, print takes an a to IO unit.' What is the actual job of the Show a => part specifically?
options: It names the one specific type, called Show, that print's argument must be
It restricts a to only those types that Haskell knows how to display — a requirement checked before print can be applied, not a description of what print does with the value
It means print always returns a String instead of performing output
It has no real effect; it is left over from an older version of the Prelude
questions.explanation: Show a => is a typeclass constraint, not a concrete type: it says 'a can be any type at all, as long as that type provides Show.' Integer, Bool, Char, and String all provide Show, which is exactly why print works on each of them without any extra setup.
optionFeedback: Show is the class being required, not the type of the argument itself — a is still a type variable, standing for whichever type actually gets used, as long as it has Show.
Correct. The constraint filters which types a is allowed to be; it says nothing about print's own result type, which remains IO ().
print's result type is IO (), exactly as the rest of the signature states; nothing about the constraint changes what print returns.
The constraint is load-bearing today, not vestigial — without Show a =>, GHC would have no way to know print can turn the value into displayable text at all.

deeper-reasoning-choosing-the-right-outp.title: Deeper reasoning: choosing the right output tool

questions.question: A student runs the program below. In the options, the lines the terminal shows are separated by a vertical bar. Which option shows the exact output, and which two lines come from different tools but look identical to the viewer?
options: Total: | 42 | 42 | 42 | 42, because each call starts on a new line and no tool ever adds quotation marks.

Total: 42 | 42 | "42" | 42. The first line is putStr followed by print on the same line. Lines two and four look the same, but one is putStrLn (show 42) and the other is putStrLn "42". The quoted "42" comes from print, which shows the String in its Haskell-readable form.
Total: 42 | 42 | 42 | 42, because print and putStrLn produce identical output for every value.
Total: | 42 | "42" | 42 | "42", because putStr and putStrLn always add quotation marks to strings.
questions.explanation: putStr leaves the cursor on the same line, so the next print continues after Total: . print x is putStrLn (show x), which is why putStrLn (show 42) and print 42 agree. print of a String shows the quotation marks, because the readable form of a String includes them, while putStrLn writes the characters directly.
optionFeedback: putStr does not end its line, so the 42 from print continues on the same line, and print "42" does include quotation marks.
Correct. Each line can be traced to a specific tool, and the one with quotation marks is the one that applied show to a String.
print and putStrLn differ whenever the value is a String: print adds the quotation marks that show produces.
Only print (through show) adds quotation marks. putStr and putStrLn write the characters of the String exactly as they are.

questions.question: A student writes two lines to display a list of marks. The first works; the second is rejected. Which explanation covers both what the first line prints and exactly why the second fails?
code: -- The last line does not compile
options: The first line prints Marks: 72,45,50. The second fails because ++ cannot be used with putStrLn.

The first line prints Marks: [72,45,50], because show turns the list into the String of its Haskell form. The second fails because ++ joins two lists of the same element type, and marks is a list of numbers while "Marks: " is a list of characters. show is the step that converts the numbers to text first.
Both lines print the same text, because Haskell converts a list of numbers to a String automatically when it is joined to text.
The first line fails, because show cannot be applied to a list, and the second line works.
questions.explanation: ++ is list concatenation: both sides must be lists of the same element type. A String is a list of characters, so a list of numbers cannot be joined to one. show produces a String describing the list, which can then be joined.
optionFeedback: show prints lists with square brackets and commas, so the brackets are part of the output. And ++ is fine with putStrLn; the problem is the types it is asked to combine.
Correct. The two lines differ only by the show call, and that call is what turns a list of numbers into text.
Haskell never converts between types implicitly. The second line is a type error.
show works on lists of numbers, which is why the first line succeeds.

questions.question: A student insists: "show 42 and print 42 are the same thing, because at the GHCi prompt both just make 42 appear." Which reply most precisely corrects the misconception, using what happens inside a program?
options: They are the same, and the student only needs to remember that print is shorter to type.

show 42 is a pure calculation that produces the String "42" and does nothing else. GHCi displays it only because the prompt echoes the value of whatever expression you type. print 42 is an IO action that actually writes to the terminal. Inside a program, show 42 on its own as a statement is rejected, because a do block needs actions, while print 42 is accepted.
show writes to the terminal and print only calculates the text, so the student has the two names the wrong way round.
They differ only in whether a newline is added: show adds one and print does not.
questions.explanation: A value and an action are different kinds of thing. GHCi's echo is a feature of the interactive prompt, which is why the distinction is invisible there and obvious in a program. print is show followed by putStrLn, so it is the action that makes the text visible.
optionFeedback: They are different kinds of thing: one is a String-producing calculation, the other an IO action. The difference matters as soon as the code is in a program.
Correct. The distinction between producing text and performing output is the central point of the lesson, and the type error for a bare show shows it concretely.
The names are reversed in this option. show performs no output at all.
Newlines are added by putStrLn and print. show has no effect on the terminal, so it adds nothing.
